§281 HazLenz presentation and active inspection cleanup

Four product-owner decisions carried out, and each one turned out to be larger
than the finding that raised it.

D-038 retires the closed /inspection cycle. §280 called it 1,511 lines; that is
the three page files. They were entry points to a whole parallel product -- a
client-side call to the engine, a browser-side PDF exporter, a device-global
offline store, a plan-tiered report packager -- and the deletion set, computed
as a strict fixpoint where a module goes only when every file that imports it
goes too, is 101 files and 13,416 lines. No capability the active workflow
requires was found in it. Nine product concepts existed only there and are
recorded rather than quietly lost: report cover fields, company logo,
confidentiality marker, tiered report packages, local PDF export, photo
annotation, the local inspection store, a 25-component HazLenz reasoning family,
and post-completion report editing.

The natural fear about that last one is the opposite

fix: make the governed cutover kill switch authoritative

GOVERNED_CUTOVER_KILL_SWITCH was a delivery brake, not an emergency stop.
It was consulted inside orchestrateShadowRequest() and nowhere else that
mattered. The two call sites that decide DURABLE state -- the controller's
resolveInspectionReleaseBinding() and inspection.service.ts's
resolveKnowledgeReleaseId() -- both read resolveCutoverEnablement(), and that
function did not know the switch existed.

Measured before the repair, under a valid GOVERNED_WITH_FALLBACK production
configuration with the switch engaged and an allowlisted principal: eligibility
still resolved GOVERNED_WITH_FALLBACK / ACCOUNT_ALLOWLISTED, a NEW inspection
was still bound to the active release, and inspection.knowledgeReleaseId was
still WRITTEN. That binding is write-once, so an operator pulling the emergency
stop mid-incident would have left permanent governed provenance behind.

Root cause was structural, not a missing check. production-shadow-authorization
imports cutover-m

feat: complete InSite v1.0 offline field readiness

Releases the §78, §79, §80 and §81 work together — the first time any of it
reaches production.

§78/§79 — Free saved history, per-user local isolation
  Free accounts can list and reopen their own saved inspections; sign-out now
  sweeps the customer content that was surviving into the next account's
  session on a shared device.

§80 — durable offline field capture
  A service-worker application shell, a per-user encrypted IndexedDB draft
  store, and explicit synchronisation, behind one new route (/field-capture).
  The guided HazLenz workspace is deliberately unchanged: analysis, risk,
  findings and reports are server-authoritative and stay ONLINE_REQUIRED, and
  nothing on the device fabricates a substitute for them.

§81 — authoritative sync idempotency
  §80 prevented duplicates by matching title + site + timestamp, which is a
  similarity judgement, not identity: it cannot separate two legitimate
  inspections created minutes apart at the same site

KG-1..KG-5D: operator commands, verification suites, evidence and documentation

The package wiring layer. Everything here depends on the five preceding commits
and nothing depends on it, so it lands last.

* Operator surface: `npm run release` (status/sources/prepare/activate/rollback)
  and `npm run review:release-record`. Activation requires the exact release id,
  the expected manifest, the expected current pointer spelled explicitly
  (including "none") and a named actor; there is no activate --latest, no prefix
  matching and no publish that bundles the lifecycle. The expected-pointer
  precondition is re-checked INSIDE the transaction under pg_advisory_xact_lock,
  because a precondition checked outside the lock is not a precondition.
  Approval stays one record at a time against an exact checksum.
* 68 verification scripts wired into backend/package.json as 65 new script
  entries. No dependency of any kind changed: ts-node remains a devDependency,
  so these are inert in a production image.
* scripts

Add refresh-token session durability; fix fabricated per-finding standard citation in reports

Auth: the 15-minute access token had no refresh mechanism, so any user
active longer than 15 minutes lost their session mid-workflow (and saw a
misleading "sign in" prompt on /pricing despite still being logged in).
Adds an opaque, rotating, DB-backed refresh token (POST /auth/refresh,
POST /auth/logout) with reuse-detection (a replayed rotated-out token
revokes the whole chain and forces re-login). apiFetch now transparently
refreshes and retries once on a 401 carrying an Authorization header, so
an active session survives token expiry without user-visible disruption;
a genuinely dead session still correctly redirects to /login. Verified
against both simulated and real (5s-lived) token expiry.

Stop a stale Pro JWT from bypassing a live-terminated subscription

EntitlementGuard checked the JWT's cached plan claim as an independent OR
alongside EntitlementService.hasFeature()'s live-subscription check, and
hasFeature() itself checked the JWT claim first too. Either path let a JWT
issued while Pro keep unlocking Pro endpoints for its full remaining
lifetime (up to JWT_EXPIRES_IN) even after Stripe had fully ended the
subscription and our webhook had already synced the termination — i.e.
"re-login required" to actually lose access, which is exactly what this
billing-lifecycle phase is required to eliminate.

Reproduced concretely with an isolated Stripe Test Clock: captured a valid
JWT while Pro, terminated the subscription (webhook confirmed synced), then
replayed the untouched old JWT against a Pro-gated endpoint and it still
passed. Confirmed fixed with the same reproduction after this change.
